steps.label: POST /api/auth/ciba/initiate
steps.description: Initiate a CIBA (Client-Initiated Backchannel Authentication) request for human approval. Client initiates a transfer that requires human review via separate device or email.

steps.label: POST /api/auth/ciba/approve-now/:authReqId
steps.description: Approve a pending transfer after human review via CIBA/HITL. Human approver grants permission for the client-initiated transfer.

spec.label: OpenID CIBA 1.0
spec.title: CIBA / HITL
spec.why: CIBA (Client-Initiated Backchannel Authentication) decouples approval from the device where a request started: the client asks the authorization server to authenticate a user, and the user approves on their own device — a push notification or app prompt — with no browser redirect anywhere in the flow. HITL (human-in-the-loop) applies the same shape to authorization: a sensitive action pauses until a named human explicitly approves it.
spec.example: You phone your bank's call center. Before the agent can discuss your account, the bank pushes an approval prompt to your mobile banking app — you tap Approve on your phone and the call proceeds. The call center never saw your password.
spec.ai: An AI agent has no browser and no human sitting next to it. CIBA is how it requests a real person's explicit approval — "approve this $500 transfer" lands on the account owner's device, and the agent stays blocked until a human answers.

steps.label: POST /api/demo/dpop/token
steps.description: Request an access token with a DPoP proof. Client sends a DPoP proof to bind the token to a specific key pair.

steps.label: POST /api/demo/dpop/verify-dpop
steps.description: Verify DPoP proof on gateway. Gateway validates that the DPoP proof is valid and matches the token being used.

spec.label: RFC 9449
spec.title: DPoP
spec.why: DPoP (Demonstrating Proof of Possession) fixes the bearer-token problem: a plain bearer token is like cash — whoever holds it can spend it. DPoP binds the access token to a private key the client keeps, and every API call must carry a fresh proof signed with that key, so the token alone is worthless to anyone who steals it.
spec.example: An access token leaks through a logging pipeline or a compromised proxy. Against a DPoP-protected API the replay fails: the attacker has the token but cannot produce the signed proof, because the private key never left the legitimate client.
spec.ai: Agent tokens pass through many hands — queues, tool servers, traces, logs. Sender-constraining them means an exfiltrated token from any of those hops cannot be replayed by whoever finds it.

steps.label: POST /api/demo/intent-binding/run
steps.description: Execute a transfer whose intent is declared via RAR authorization_details (RFC 9396) — PingOne Authorize evaluates the requested amount against the agent's declared $100 intent cap and returns PERMIT or DENY.

spec.label: RFC 9396
spec.title: RAR
spec.why: RAR (Rich Authorization Requests) replaces coarse scopes with structured authorization_details — type, amount, account, action — so the authorization server grants exactly one described transaction, and policy can enforce the difference between what was asked and what was granted.
spec.example: Instead of a token with a broad payments scope, the token says "one transfer, up to $100, from checking, to this payee". A $2,000 transfer attempt with that token is denied by policy, not by hoping the client behaves.
spec.ai: The agent declares its intent up front in machine-checkable form. Here PingOne Authorize compares the amount the agent actually requests against its declared $100 intent cap and returns PERMIT or DENY — overreach is caught at the policy layer.

steps.label: POST /api/demo/par/par
steps.description: Push an authorization request for later retrieval. Client sends authorization parameters and receives a request_uri for later use.

steps.label: POST /api/demo/par/authorize
steps.description: Authorize a pushed authorization request. Authorization server processes the request_uri and issues an authorization code.

spec.label: RFC 9126
spec.title: PAR
spec.why: PAR (Pushed Authorization Requests) moves authorization parameters off the front channel: normally they travel through the browser as a query string — visible, tamperable, logged in history. With PAR the client pushes them directly to the authorization server over an authenticated backchannel and receives a one-time request_uri; the redirect carries only that opaque reference.
spec.example: Like handing your paperwork to the bank clerk in person and getting a ticket number, instead of writing your account details on a postcard that passes through every intermediate hand. A malicious browser extension that rewrites redirect URLs has nothing to rewrite.
spec.ai: The intent of the flow is fixed and integrity-protected before anything user-facing happens — an agent (or anything between it and the AS) cannot quietly alter scope, redirect target, or amount mid-redirect.

steps.label: POST /api/pf-ai-agent/rar/start
steps.title: Push the request and get the sign-in URL
steps.description: Push the request with its authorization_details (RAR, RFC 9396) over PAR and get back the URL the user opens to sign in and approve. Send {"format":"json"} to receive that URL and the redacted trace as JSON; without it the answer is the 302 the app's own page follows. Open authorizeUrl in a browser tab, sign in and approve, then run step 2.

steps.label: GET /api/pf-ai-agent/status
steps.title: Read the result
steps.description: After the user has signed in and approved, read the outcome: accepted or denied, the token type, and the redacted trace of every hop. rarResult is null until the run completes.

spec.label: RFC 9396
spec.title: RAR (PingFederate)
spec.why: RAR (Rich Authorization Requests) lets a client ask for one precise action instead of a broad scope: a banking_transaction detail naming the accounts, the amount and the currency. PingFederate checks that detail against policy while the user signs in, and the token that comes back covers only what was approved. The request is pushed over PAR first, so the details never travel in a browser URL.
spec.example: An agent asks to move $125 from checking to savings. PingFederate compares the amount and accounts with the user's limits; an out-of-policy request is refused before any token exists.
spec.ai: An agent should hold authority for the one action it was asked to do, not a standing scope. RAR is how that action is written down and enforced at the authorization server.

steps.label: POST /api/pf-ai-agent/cross-domain/exchange
steps.title: Get a PingFederate ID-JAG and redeem it
steps.description: The client trades its PingFederate access token for an ID-JAG that PingFederate signs (the issuer is PingFederate's own), checks the assertion, then redeems it at the third-party authorization server for an access token scoped to that domain. One call runs both hops; the response is the redacted trace of each, with the ID-JAG claims decoded.

spec.label: App-Driven AuthZ
spec.title: XAA / ID-JAG (PingFederate)
spec.why: XAA / ID-JAG covers cross-domain delegation: a client with an identity in its home domain exchanges its token for an ID-JAG assertion the target domain's authorization server accepts, with no shared user store and no second login. Here the home domain is PingFederate, so the assertion's issuer is PingFederate and its signature is checked against PingFederate's published key.
spec.example: Airline status getting you into a partner lounge: the partner does not have you in its member database; it accepts an assertion from your airline and issues its own lounge pass.
spec.ai: An agent working across two companies' APIs gets a per-domain token in each, every one traceable to the same home identity that delegated the task.

steps.label: POST /api/pf-ai-agent/token-exchange/agent
steps.title: Exchange the user token for an agent token
steps.description: First exchange: the signed-in user's PingFederate token plus the AI agent's own actor token go to PingFederate, which returns a token for the agent gateway. The sub is still the user; act names the agent. The response carries the new token's claims, never the token.

steps.label: POST /api/pf-ai-agent/token-exchange/mcp
steps.title: Exchange the agent token for an MCP token
steps.description: Second exchange: the agent token plus the MCP service's actor token go to PingFederate, which returns the token the MCP server accepts. The act claim is now nested: the MCP service acting for the agent acting for the user.

spec.label: RFC 8693
spec.title: RFC 8693 Token Exchange (PingFederate)
spec.why: Token Exchange (RFC 8693) trades one token for another at the authorization server: a narrower audience, narrower scope, and an act claim recording who is acting on whose behalf. Here PingFederate runs two hops, user to agent and agent to MCP service, and the final token carries a nested act chain naming both actors. Needs a PingFederate sign-in.
spec.example: A valet key: starts the car, will not open the trunk. Each downstream call gets a token minted for exactly that call, so a compromised service holds a token good for almost nothing.
spec.ai: Every agent hop is a fresh exchange, so the token that reaches a tool server is scoped to that one call, and the nested act chain is a record of every delegation.

steps.label: POST /api/pf-ai-agent/ciba/start
steps.title: Start the approval request
steps.description: Start a CIBA approval request for the signed-in user at PingFederate. The client names the user and a binding message; PingFederate asks that user to approve on their own device.

steps.label: POST /api/pf-ai-agent/ciba/mock-decision
steps.title: Approve on the mock phone
steps.description: The approver answers. Only the mock phone can be answered from here; with a real device the user taps Approve there, and this step answers 404 (pf_ai_ciba_mock_disabled).

steps.label: GET /api/pf-ai-agent/ciba/status
steps.title: Poll the result
steps.description: Poll the request. Returns pending until the approver answers, then approved or denied with safe metadata only (subject, issuer, scope); never the auth_req_id or a token.

spec.label: OpenID CIBA 1.0
spec.title: CIBA / HITL (PingFederate)
spec.why: CIBA decouples approval from the device where a request started: the client asks the authorization server to authenticate a user, and the user approves on their own device with no browser redirect. This is the PingFederate run of the flow; it needs a PingFederate sign-in, and with the mock phone enabled no PingFederate call is made at all.
spec.ai: An AI agent has no browser and no human beside it. CIBA is how it asks the account owner for explicit approval of a specific action and stays blocked until a person answers.

steps.label: POST /api/pf-ai-agent/par/start
steps.title: Push the request and get the sign-in URL
steps.description: Push the authorization request to PingFederate over PAR and get back the sign-in URL. The browser URL carries only the client and a one-time request_uri; the parameters travelled server to server. Open authorizeUrl in a browser tab, sign in, then run step 2.

steps.label: GET /api/pf-ai-agent/par/result
steps.title: Read the result
steps.description: After the user has signed in and approved, read the outcome: the code exchange result and the redacted trace of each hop. state is none until a run completes.

spec.label: RFC 9126
spec.title: PAR (PingFederate)
spec.why: PAR (Pushed Authorization Requests) moves the authorization request out of the browser URL: the client POSTs its parameters to the authorization server directly and gets back a one-time request_uri to put in the redirect. Nothing in the URL can be tampered with, and the request is authenticated before the user sees anything. This is a real push to PingFederate's PAR endpoint.
spec.example: Instead of writing your order on a postcard anyone can read or alter on the way, you hand it to the clerk and carry only a ticket number.
spec.ai: An agent's request for access can be sealed and checked at the server before any human is asked to approve it, so a tampered or forged request never reaches the approval screen.

steps.label: POST /api/pf-ai-agent/pkce/start
steps.title: Start the sign-in with a code challenge
steps.description: Start an authorization-code sign-in at PingFederate with PKCE: the client keeps a random verifier, sends only its SHA-256 challenge, and later proves it holds the verifier when it redeems the code. Open authorizeUrl in a browser tab, sign in, then run step 2.

steps.label: GET /api/pf-ai-agent/pkce/result
steps.title: Read the result
steps.description: After the user has signed in, read the outcome: who PingFederate says signed in and the redacted trace including the code redemption with the verifier. state is none until done.

spec.label: RFC 7636
spec.title: PKCE (PingFederate)
spec.why: PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange) stops a stolen authorization code from being useful: the client invents a random secret, sends only its hash with the authorization request, and must present the original secret to redeem the code. This is a real PKCE sign-in at PingFederate, using a client identified by a metadata document URL.
spec.example: A coat-check ticket with a torn corner: only the person holding the matching half can collect the coat, even if someone else picks up the ticket.
spec.ai: Agents and apps that cannot keep a client secret still get a code flow that is safe to run: an intercepted code is worthless without the verifier that never left the client.

steps.label: POST /api/pf-ai-agent/dpop/start
steps.title: Start the sign-in with a DPoP key
steps.description: Start the same request with DPoP: the client generates a fresh key pair, PingFederate is told to require DPoP for this client, and the access token that comes back is bound to the public key's thumbprint. Open authorizeUrl in a browser tab, sign in, then run step 2.

steps.label: GET /api/pf-ai-agent/dpop/result
steps.title: Read the result
steps.description: After the user has signed in and approved, read the outcome: the token type (DPoP) and the public key thumbprint the token is bound to. state is none until a run completes.

spec.label: RFC 9449
spec.title: DPoP (PingFederate)
spec.why: DPoP (Demonstrating Proof of Possession) fixes the bearer-token problem: a plain bearer token is like cash, whoever holds it can spend it. DPoP binds the access token to a private key the client keeps, and every use must carry a fresh signed proof. Here PingFederate requires DPoP for the client and returns a token of type DPoP bound to the key's thumbprint.
spec.example: An access token leaks through a logging pipeline or a compromised proxy. Against a DPoP-protected API the replay fails: the attacker has the token but cannot produce the signed proof, because the private key never left the legitimate client.
spec.ai: Agent tokens pass through many hands: queues, tool servers, traces, logs. Sender-constraining them means an exfiltrated token from any of those hops cannot be replayed by whoever finds it.

steps.label: POST /api/demo/pkce/authorize
steps.description: Client sends its PKCE code_challenge to obtain an authorization code.

steps.label: POST /api/demo/pkce/token
steps.description: Client redeems the code with its code_verifier — server recomputes the challenge from the verifier and only issues a token if the derived code matches the one step 1 returned for that challenge.

spec.label: RFC 7636
spec.title: PKCE
spec.why: PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange) protects the authorization code, which travels back through a redirect other software on the device can observe. The client invents a one-time secret, sends only its hash (code_challenge) when the flow starts, and must present the original (code_verifier) to redeem the code — so an intercepted code is useless on its own.
spec.example: A coat-check ticket that only matches your stub. A rogue app on your phone registers the same redirect scheme and captures the authorization code — and gets nothing, because it cannot produce the verifier that hashes to the challenge. Mandatory for public clients in OAuth 2.1.
spec.ai: Any agent running where it cannot keep a client secret — a desktop, a container image someone can inspect — is a public client. PKCE is what makes its code flow safe without a secret.

steps.label: POST /api/privilege-mcp/auth/start
steps.description: POST /auth/start — begin the OAuth PKCE flow against the Privilege AI Gateway.

steps.label: GET /api/privilege-mcp/auth/callback
steps.description: GET /auth/callback — exchange the authorization code for the gateway's token.

spec.label: RFC 7591 Dynamic Client Registration
spec.title: Privilege AI Gateway sign-in
spec.why: The PingOne Privilege AI Gateway is its own authorization server, and it registers callers dynamically rather than from a client id you configure ahead of time: the client discovers the gateway, registers itself (RFC 7591), then runs Authorization Code with PKCE (RFC 7636). Two consequences shape everything downstream. The token it issues is OPAQUE, so there are no claims to decode — introspection is the only way to inspect it. And it is bound to ONE Agentic App: presenting a token minted for another app is refused before routing even happens, which is why each door needs its own sign-in.
spec.example: A visitor badge that only opens one building. It proves who you are and it was issued on the spot rather than pre-arranged, but showing it at a different building gets you turned away at the door, not at the meeting room.
spec.ai: An agent reaching a tool behind Privilege cannot carry one credential everywhere. It registers with the gateway, signs its user in once per application, and the gateway decides per app and per tool whether that human is allowed — before the agent's own gateway ever evaluates scopes.

steps.label: GET /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/metadata
steps.description: Client discovers this API's protected-resource metadata — which authorization server issues its tokens and which scopes it accepts.

steps.label: GET /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/all
steps.description: Client extends discovery to every downstream MCP resource server so it can see the full set of authorization servers and scopes across the chain before attempting a token request.

spec.label: RFC 9728
spec.title: Resource Metadata
spec.why: Protected Resource Metadata (RFC 9728) lets an API publish a .well-known document declaring which authorization server issues its tokens and which scopes it accepts. Clients discover how to authorize against a resource instead of being hand-configured for it.
spec.example: This is how MCP authorization bootstraps: an MCP client hits a protected server, gets a 401 pointing at the resource metadata, reads which authorization server to use, and starts the right OAuth flow — zero out-of-band setup. Like a door that lists which badge office issues the badges it accepts.
spec.ai: Agents connect to tool servers they have never seen before. Discovery metadata is what lets that happen safely at runtime instead of via config files written by a human in advance.

steps.label: GET /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/metadata/pingfederate
steps.title: Discover the authorization server
steps.description: The same document with PingFederate as the authorization server: the issuer is the configured PF_ISSUER, so a client discovering this API is sent to PingFederate.

spec.label: RFC 9728
spec.title: Resource Metadata (PingFederate)
spec.why: Protected Resource Metadata (RFC 9728) lets an API publish a .well-known document declaring which authorization server issues its tokens and which scopes it accepts. Here the declared authorization server is PingFederate, so a client that discovers this API is sent to PingFederate's issuer instead of PingOne's.
spec.example: This is how MCP authorization bootstraps: an MCP client hits a protected server, gets a 401 pointing at the resource metadata, reads which authorization server to use, and starts the right OAuth flow with zero out-of-band setup.
spec.ai: Agents connect to tool servers they have never seen before. Discovery metadata is what lets that happen safely at runtime instead of via config files written by a human in advance.

steps.label: POST /api/demo/rfc8693/token
steps.description: Exchange delegated token via RFC 8693 token exchange. Client sends a subject token (typically an ID token) and requests an access token.

steps.label: POST /api/demo/rfc8693/introspect
steps.description: Validate and introspect the delegated token via RFC 8693. Token exchanger verifies the subject token and returns token details.

spec.label: RFC 8693
spec.title: RFC 8693 Token Exchange
spec.why: Token Exchange (RFC 8693) trades one token for another at the authorization server: narrower audience, narrower scope, and an act claim recording who is acting on whose behalf. No service ever forwards the user's original token — each hop gets a token minted for exactly that hop.
spec.example: A valet key: starts the car, will not open the trunk. In a microservice chain, the gateway exchanges the user's token for a service-scoped token per downstream call, so a compromised downstream service holds a token good for almost nothing.
spec.ai: This is the backbone of this demo. Every agent hop — BFF to agent, agent to MCP — is a fresh exchange, so the token that reaches a tool server is scoped to that one call, and the nested act chain is a cryptographic audit trail of every delegation.

steps.label: POST /api/demo/spiffe/svid
steps.description: Demo workload requests a JWT-SVID from the local mock issuer using its registered workload ID and matching selectors. This P1 flow performs no runtime workload attestation.

steps.label: POST /api/demo/spiffe/verify
steps.description: Peer workload validates the presented SVID against the expected trust domain before accepting the call.

spec.label: SPIFFE Bearer Token
spec.title: SPIFFE
spec.why: Real SPIFFE uses workload attestation to issue short-lived identities without distributing long-lived secrets. This P1 demo instead uses a local mock issuer that accepts only registered workload IDs with matching selector values; it does not attest the caller at runtime.
spec.example: The demo is like a training badge desk that checks a requested name and department against a registration list before issuing a short-lived badge. The supplied selectors must match, but the desk does not independently inspect or attest the workload presenting them.
spec.ai: Agent fleets benefit from short-lived workload identities and cryptographic verification. This P1 flow demonstrates those token and trust checks with a local mock issuer and registered selectors, not runtime workload attestation.

steps.label: POST /api/demo/txn-tokens/request
steps.description: Edge service requests a txn-token from the Transaction Token Service, carrying the caller's subject token and the request context to bind.

steps.label: POST /api/demo/txn-tokens/propagate
steps.description: A downstream microservice receives the txn-token on the next hop, validates it, and re-mints a fresh one to propagate further inward.

spec.label: Transaction Tokens
spec.title: TXN Tokens
spec.why: Transaction Tokens pin the context of one request: the edge service swaps the caller's token for a short-lived txn-token recording who called, what they asked for, and which workload chain handled it. Every internal hop can verify the original request context instead of trusting whoever called it last.
spec.example: A numbered work order stapled to a job as it moves through a shop floor: any station can check what was actually ordered, rather than trusting the previous station's word for it. A compromised internal service cannot invent a "transfer $10,000" job from a "check balance" request.
spec.ai: Agent requests fan out across many internal services. A txn-token makes the original human request travel with the work, so deep services enforce against what the user actually asked — not what an intermediate agent claims they asked.

steps.label: POST /api/demo/xaa/id-jag
steps.description: Client exchanges its home-domain ID token for an ID-JAG assertion scoped to the target (foreign) domain's authorization server.

steps.label: POST /api/demo/xaa/token
steps.description: Foreign domain's AS trades the ID-JAG assertion for an access token scoped to its own resource server (JWT-bearer grant, RFC 7523 shape).

spec.label: App-Driven AuthZ
spec.title: XAA / ID-JAG
spec.why: XAA / ID-JAG covers cross-domain delegation: a client with an identity in its home domain exchanges its ID token for an ID-JAG assertion the target domain's authorization server accepts — cross-company access rooted in one home identity, with no shared user store and no second login.
spec.example: Airline status getting you into a partner lounge: the partner does not have you in its member database — it accepts an assertion from your airline and issues its own lounge pass. Here, the foreign domain's AS mints its own access token from the ID-JAG.
spec.ai: An agent working across two companies' APIs — booking travel, filing an insurance claim — gets a per-domain token in each, every one traceable to the same home identity that delegated the task.
